```{r load}
source("R/metrics.R")
source("R/decision.R")
source("R/plotting.R")
x <- readRDS("data/credit.rds")
cv <- readRDS("results/cv.rds")
tst <- readRDS("results/test.rds")
y_tr <- cv$y
y_te <- tst$y
E_tr <- pmax(x$BILL_AMT1[!cv$is_test], 0)
E_te <- pmax(x$BILL_AMT1[cv$is_test], 0)
late_te <- x$PAY_1[cv$is_test] >= 2
pi_tr <- mean(y_tr)
pct <- function(v, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * v)
f3 <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f", v)
```

A score is only useful once it changes what the bank does. This page sets the
decision rule from the costs, checks it against the data, and compares the
models by the economic value they would produce under a stylised model of the
bank's intervention. The value is simulated, not observed: the data record what
happened without intervention, and what a client would have done after a limit
cut or a frozen card cannot be seen.

## Decision rule

In September the bank can either keep an account as it is or act on it: cut
the limit, freeze the card, start collection early. In this stylised model,
acting is assumed to remove the exposure, so it neither earns nor loses
anything. This is optimistic: freezing a card stops new spending but does not
erase the balance already owed. Keeping the account earns
a margin if the client repays and loses the defaulted amount otherwise. Per unit
of exposure, with the loss given default as the unit of cost:

| | client repays | client defaults |
|---|---|---|
| keep | $+r$ | $-1$ |
| act | $0$ | $0$ |

The cost ratio $r$ is what the bank gives up by acting on a good client,
relative to what a default costs. A client with default probability $p$ is
worth $(1 - p)\,r - p$ per unit of exposure if kept, so the bank should act when

$$
p > t(r) = \frac{r}{1 + r}.
$$

The exposure cancels out: the threshold is the same for every client, and only
the probability matters. This is where calibration enters. A model whose 20%
does not mean 20% would apply the wrong threshold, however well it ranks
clients.

The exposure is the September balance, set to zero when it is negative. The
model is deliberately simple: acting rarely removes the whole exposure, and a
good client who is acted on may be lost for longer than a month. Both effects
change $r$ rather than the form of the rule, so results are given over a range
of $r$ instead of for a single guess.

Three values of $r$ are used as reference points:

| $r$ | threshold | reading |
|---|---|---|
| 0.10 | `r pct(cost_threshold(0.10))` | a default costs ten times as much as losing a good client |
| 0.25 | `r pct(cost_threshold(0.25))` | four times as much |
| 0.50 | `r pct(cost_threshold(0.50))` | twice as much |

## Does the theory hold on the data?

If the probabilities are calibrated, the threshold that maximises the value on
past data should be close to $t(r)$. The table compares the two on the training
set, out of fold, searching thresholds on a grid of step 0.005.

```{r empirical-threshold}
rs <- c(0.10, 0.25, 0.50)
et <- t(sapply(rs, function(r) c(
  r = r,
  theory = cost_threshold(r),
  logit = best_threshold(y_tr, tst$oof$logit, E_tr, r),
  xgb = best_threshold(y_tr, tst$oof$xgb, E_tr, r)
)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  `cost ratio r` = sprintf("%.2f", et[, "r"]),
  `t(r)` = f3(et[, "theory"]),
  `best threshold, logistic` = f3(et[, "logit"]),
  `best threshold, XGBoost` = f3(et[, "xgb"]),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "rrrr")
```

The best thresholds found on the data are within a few points of the
theoretical ones, and none is systematically above or below. The thresholds
below are therefore set from $r$ alone, and nothing is tuned on the test set.

The balanced accuracy and Youden's index used in the original version of this
project are a special case. Maximising balanced accuracy gives a missed default
a weight $1/n_1$ and a false alarm a weight $1/n_0$, which is the cost ratio
$r = n_1 / n_0 = `r f3(pi_tr / (1 - pi_tr))`$ and, for a calibrated model, the
threshold $t = \pi = `r f3(pi_tr)`$, the default rate. Youden's threshold is
not neutral: it fixes the costs implicitly, and they are counted per client
rather than per unit of exposure.

## Simulated value on the test set

```{r value-setup}
policies <- function(r) {
  t <- cost_threshold(r)
  cbind(
    keep_all = rep(FALSE, length(y_te)),
    act_all = rep(TRUE, length(y_te)),
    rule = late_te,
    logit = tst$pred$logit > t,
    xgb = tst$pred$xgb > t,
    oracle = y_te == 1
  )
}
contrib <- function(r) {
  A <- policies(r)
  apply(A, 2, function(act) (!act) * ((1 - y_te) * r - y_te) * E_te)
}
set.seed(3)
B <- 1000
W <- rmultinom(B, length(y_te), rep(1, length(y_te)))   # bootstrap counts, n x B

# Value of each policy as a share of what perfect foresight adds over the better
# of the two policies that need no model (keep everyone, act on everyone).
captured <- function(V) {
  base <- pmax(V[, "keep_all"], V[, "act_all"])
  (V[, c("rule", "logit", "xgb"), drop = FALSE] - base) / (V[, "oracle"] - base)
}
```

Each policy is scored by its simulated value relative to two references. The floor is
the better of the two policies that need no model, keeping everyone or acting on
everyone, since a model has to beat both. The ceiling is perfect foresight:
acting on exactly the clients who will default. The share of the distance
between floor and ceiling that a policy covers is reported, with a 95% bootstrap
interval over test clients.

```{r value-table}
lab <- c(rule = "Rule PAY_1 >= 2", logit = "Logistic regression", xgb = "XGBoost")
vt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rs, function(r) {
  C <- contrib(r)
  point <- captured(matrix(colSums(C), nrow = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(C))))
  boot <- captured(t(W) %*% C)
  A <- policies(r)
  data.frame(
    r = sprintf("%.2f", r),
    policy = lab,
    `clients acted on` = pct(colMeans(A[, names(lab)])),
    `precision` = pct(sapply(names(lab), function(m) mean(y_te[A[, m]]))),
    `recall` = pct(sapply(names(lab), function(m) sum(A[, m] & y_te == 1) / sum(y_te))),
    `value captured` = pct(point[1, ]),
    `95% interval` = sapply(names(lab), function(m) {
      q <- quantile(boot[, m], c(0.025, 0.975)); sprintf("[%s, %s]", pct(q[1]), pct(q[2]))
    }),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(vt, row.names = FALSE, align = "rlrrrrr")
```

Precision and recall are in the table only as a description. They are not
chosen: they follow from the cost ratio. Asking whether a precision of 35% is
acceptable has no answer until $r$ is known, and once it is known the threshold
follows.

```{r sensitivity, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.2}
r_grid <- exp(seq(log(0.05), log(1), length.out = 40))
curves <- lapply(r_grid, function(r) {
  C <- contrib(r)
  point <- captured(matrix(colSums(C), nrow = 1, dimnames = list(NULL, colnames(C))))
  boot <- t(W) %*% C
  cb <- captured(boot)
  d <- cb[, "xgb"] - cb[, "logit"]
  list(
    boot_diff = d,
    curve = data.frame(r = r, policy = lab, value = point[1, ],
                       lo = apply(cb, 2, quantile, 0.025), hi = apply(cb, 2, quantile, 0.975)),
    diff = data.frame(r = r, value = point[1, "xgb"] - point[1, "logit"],
                      lo = quantile(d, 0.025), hi = quantile(d, 0.975))
  )
})
cd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(curves, `[[`, "curve"))
dd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(curves, `[[`, "diff"))
cd$policy <- factor(cd$policy, levels = lab)
cols <- setNames(unname(palette_main[c("grey", "accent", "dark")]), lab)

p1 <- ggplot(cd, aes(r, value, colour = policy, fill = policy)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = pi_tr / (1 - pi_tr), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = pi_tr / (1 - pi_tr), y = -0.25, label = "Youden", hjust = -0.1, size = 3, colour = "grey35") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_axis) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) + scale_fill_manual(values = cols) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.3, 0.7)) +
  labs(title = "Simulated value captured on the test set",
       subtitle = "Share of the gap between no model and perfect foresight",
       x = "Cost ratio r (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_report()

p2 <- ggplot(dd, aes(r, value)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = palette_main["light"], alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(colour = palette_main["dark"], linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_axis) +
  labs(title = "XGBoost minus logistic",
       subtitle = "Paired 95% interval",
       x = "Cost ratio r (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_report()

patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, widths = c(1.5, 1))
```

```{r numbers}
low <- dd$r < 0.15
mid <- dd$r > 0.2 & dd$r < 0.6
BD <- sapply(curves, `[[`, "boot_diff")   # bootstrap replicates x cost ratios
region <- function(sel) {
  q <- quantile(rowMeans(BD[, sel, drop = FALSE]), c(0.025, 0.975))
  c(mean = mean(dd$value[sel]), lo = q[[1]], hi = q[[2]])
}
reg_low <- region(low)
reg_mid <- region(mid)
pts <- function(v) sprintf("%+.1f", 100 * v)
```

Three findings.

**The models beat the policies that need none over almost the whole range.**
They capture up to `r pct(max(cd$value[cd$policy != lab["rule"]]), 0)` of what
perfect foresight would add, most near the middle of the range, where keeping
everyone and acting on everyone are both poor. The rule `PAY_1 >= 2` acts on
the same `r pct(mean(late_te))` of clients whatever the costs, and when
defaults are expensive it does worse than having no model at all.

**Which model is worth more depends on the costs.** The right panel gives the
paired bootstrap difference between the two models at each cost ratio. These
intervals are pointwise, so they are summarised by region, again with a paired
bootstrap over test clients, averaging the difference over the cost ratios of
the region in each replicate.

| region | average difference, XGBoost minus logistic | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|
| $r < 0.15$ | `r pts(reg_low["mean"])` points | [`r pts(reg_low["lo"])`, `r pts(reg_low["hi"])`] |
| $0.2 < r < 0.6$ | `r pts(reg_mid["mean"])` points | [`r pts(reg_mid["lo"])`, `r pts(reg_mid["hi"])`] |

When acting is cheap compared with a default, the decision is about finding the
clients safe enough to keep, at the bottom of the risk scale, and there
XGBoost is ahead`r if (reg_low["lo"] > 0) "" else " on average, though the interval includes zero"`.
In the middle of the range, around the point Youden's threshold corresponds to,
the logistic regression is slightly ahead`r if (reg_mid["hi"] < 0) "" else ", though the interval includes zero"`.
XGBoost's better log loss comes from better probabilities on average, and only
the probabilities near $t(r)$ change a decision.

The two regions were drawn after looking at this curve on the test set, so the
intervals above are not those of a test fixed in advance. Part 5 checks whether
the same pattern appears on other splits of the data.

**The choice between the two models is a business decision.** For a bank
whose cost ratio lies in the middle range, the logistic regression does at
least as well as XGBoost on this test set, and it is additive, readable and
cheaper to validate and monitor. For a bank that acts at low thresholds, XGBoost is the
better candidate.
Part 6 looks at what each model has learned.

## Limits

- The value is simulated under a stylised intervention model, not a profit
  the bank would have realised. The effect of an intervention cannot be
  observed in these data, and acting is assumed to remove the whole exposure.
- The cost model is linear and static. In practice acting on an account
  recovers only part of the exposure, and the loss given default and the margin
  vary across clients. A richer model would change $r$ client by client but not
  the logic of comparing a calibrated probability with a cost ratio.
- The value is measured on one test set of `r format(length(y_te), big.mark = ",")`
  clients. The intervals account for which clients were drawn, not for the
  randomness of training, which part 5 addresses.
- The data come from a single bank in 2005, a year of severe credit card
  delinquency in Taiwan, with a default rate of `r pct(pi_tr)`. The cost ratios
  at which acting on everyone beats keeping everyone reflect that rate.
